title: Hierarchical reinforcement learning and subgoals
matchup: Dayan and Hinton (1992) and LeCun (2022) vs Schmidhuber's subgoal generators (1990 to 1992)
question: Do Schmidhuber's 1990-92 subgoal generators establish the priority he claims for later hierarchical reinforcement learning and LeCun's planning proposal?

usual_credit.summary: Dayan and Hinton's "Feudal Reinforcement Learning" (NIPS 1992) describes a Q-learning managerial hierarchy in which high-level managers set tasks for sub-managers, who learn to satisfy them. Sutton, Precup and Singh (1999) introduced the options framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning. In 2022 LeCun's position paper "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence" named the learning of hierarchical representations of percepts and action plans at multiple time scales as one of three main challenges for AI research, and it proposed a hierarchical joint-embedding architecture in which the abstract actions inferred at a high level define subgoals for the level below.

works.who: Richard S. Sutton, Doina Precup and Satinder Singh
works.title: Between MDPs and semi-MDPs: a framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning
A path towards autonomous machine intelligence (version 0.9.2)

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that his 1990-92 work already described differentiable subgoal generation for hierarchical control. A controller receives start and goal commands, an evaluator learns the cost of moving between them, and a recurrent generator learns intermediate subgoals using the evaluator's gradients. He says Dayan and Hinton's feudal reinforcement learning did not cite this work, and that LeCun's 2022 hierarchical-planning proposal repeats the same principle without credit. His objection concerns both technical continuity and the presentation of hierarchical planning as a research challenge, although demonstrating one formulation does not establish that every later planning problem was solved.

quotes.text: Lecun (@ylecun)’s 2022 paper on Autonomous Machine Intelligence rehashes but doesn’t cite essential work of 1990-2015.
already in 1990, this problem was at least partially solved through my Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) with end-to-end differentiable NN-based subgoal generators
I published exactly this over 3 decades ago: a controller NN gets extra command inputs of the form (start, goal).
This work did not cite Schmidhuber's gradient-based subgoal generators for hierarchical reinforcement learning (1990).[HRL0-2]
solves (at least in principle) what has been called an "open problem" in 2022.

response.summary: LeCun's 2022 position paper says that it claims priority for none of its component ideas and proposes assembling them into a consistent architecture. Its planning discussion traces the use of a higher-level action as a condition for a lower level to control theory. In a [December 2022 interview](https://analyticsindiamag.com/ai-features/angels-demons-of-ai), LeCun argues that making ideas work at scale is a contribution distinct from proposing an initial idea. The linked sources contain no specific answer by Dayan or Hinton about the subgoal-generator citations, so these positions should not be treated as a joint reply from all later authors.

quotes.text: The idea that an action is merely a condition to be satisfied by the level below is actually an old one in control theory.

quotes.text: He has an unusual idea about how credit should be attributed.

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber's technical report FKI-129-90 appeared in 1990, his paper "Learning to generate sub-goals for action sequences" in 1991, and his paper with Wahnsiedler on neural subgoal generators in the 1993 proceedings of SAB 1992.

Dayan and Hinton's "Feudal Reinforcement Learning" appeared in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 5, and Sutton, Precup and Singh's options paper appeared in Artificial Intelligence in 1999.

LeCun's paper of 27 June 2022 lists learning hierarchical representations and plans at multiple levels of abstraction and time scales as one of three main challenges and proposes a hierarchical joint-embedding architecture for planning.
Schmidhuber announced his critique of LeCun's paper on X on 7 July 2022.
crux: The sources differ on whether a controller with (start, goal) command inputs and a learned subgoal generator is the same idea as the later feudal, options and hierarchical joint-embedding formulations or one of several independent routes to temporal abstraction, which LeCun's paper itself traces in part to control theory. They also differ on whether later authors knew of the 1990 to 1992 reports and should have cited them.

card.headline: Hierarchical reinforcement learning
card.question: Did his 1990-92 subgoal generators already contain the hierarchical planning idea of later work?
card.claim: He says his 1990-92 networks learned to generate subgoals between a start and a goal, and that Dayan, Hinton and LeCun did not cite them.
card.pushback: LeCun's 2022 paper claims priority for none of its parts and traces subgoal-style planning to control theory, while Dayan and Hinton have not replied.
card.crux: The question is whether learning subgoals from start and goal inputs is the same idea as later feudal and hierarchical planning methods.
